opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Brenda, thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, and we don't work for any company, union or party. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All right. I'm not much of a talker, but I'll do my best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I hope that's how it goes. I'd probably keep it to myself at work, though. People there are touchy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even in that picture, the coding software keeps getting better. It already suggests the codes and I check them. So I'd still wonder how long they need two of us checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down. Do my numbers, don't make mistakes, and keep paying off the car. Maybe put a little aside if my son chips in more for groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm a worrier, always have been.

S0.say: I hope that's how it goes. I'd mostly keep it to myself at work.
S0.think: Even here the coding software keeps improving, so she wonders how long they'll need two people checking.
S0.do: Keeps her head down, avoids mistakes, and puts a little aside if her son chips in more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been through changes before. We went from paper to computers and I learned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But I was 30 then. Now I'm 56. If they hire fewer beginners, fine, but they'll also let the older ones retire and not replace them. And I'm not near enough to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor straight out if there's a plan for our team. And I'd look at the audit side, checking the computer's codes, since somebody has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. Like waiting for a test result.

S1.say: We've been through changes before. We went from paper to computers and I learned it.
S1.think: At 56 she's too far from retirement, and she expects older staff to be let go without replacement.
S1.do: Asks her supervisor directly about the team's future and looks at moving into auditing the software's codes.
S1.feel: Nervous, like waiting for a test result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who've done this job for twenty years deserve a chance to retrain, not a box and a security guard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said retraining. If they offered it, what would you want to retrain as?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. That's the trouble. I'd want something with steady hours and no selling. Maybe patient scheduling, if that's not gone too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be in the first round. Routine office work is exactly what I do. There's nothing else like it in this town, and I'm not moving at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything. No eating out, cancel the streaming, talk to my son about paying more of the bills. I'd apply for front desk work at the clinics, anything with health insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I don't sleep well already, and this would make it worse.

S2.say: People who've done this job for twenty years deserve a chance to retrain, not a box and a security guard.
S2.think: She expects to be in the first round of cuts, with nothing similar in town and no plan to move.
S2.do: Cuts all extras, asks her son to cover more bills, and applies for clinic front desk jobs with health insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not say much. Everyone would be in the same boat and nobody wants to hear another sad story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be out, no question. And I'm not one of the people whose house is worth more. I rent. So the boom does nothing for me but push up my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apply for anything, cleaning, care work, a till at the supermarket. Take unemployment while I look. I'd ask my son if we can manage on his wages for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overwhelmed. Like there's no ground under me.

S3.say: Wouldn't say much, since everyone would be in the same boat.
S3.think: She'd be out for sure, and as a renter the boom only pushes up her rent.
S3.do: Applies for any job, including cleaning, care work and supermarket tills, claims unemployment, and leans on her son's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what are people supposed to do now? Even the jobs we told each other to fall back on are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the last one I thought I could at least clean or do care work. If the robots take that too, there's nothing left for someone like me. I'm too young to retire and too old to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but faster, and I'd stop being picky. I'd go to the church food bank if I had to. I'd look into whether the government has some sort of help for older workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeless, to be honest. Like the doors keep shutting.

S4.say: What are people supposed to do now? Even the jobs we told each other to fall back on are going.
S4.think: Her backup plan of cleaning or care work disappears too. Too young to retire, too old to start over.
S4.do: Takes any job faster, uses the church food bank if needed, and looks for government help for older workers.
S4.feel: Hopeless, like the doors keep shutting.
